Polynomials and algebraic numbers

Source: vignettes/polynomials.Rmd
polynomials.Rmd

The polynomial module is the engine under much of symcompR: factoring, cancellation, partial fractions, root finding, and integration of rational functions all reduce to polynomial arithmetic. This vignette shows the Poly class, division and GCDs, factorization over different domains, Groebner bases, resultants, roots, Galois groups, and algebraic number theory.

library(symcompR)
x <- Symbol("x"); y <- Symbol("y")
a <- Symbol("a"); b <- Symbol("b"); c <- Symbol("c")

The Poly class

Poly() converts an expression into a polynomial in the given generators with coefficients in a domain. The domain is inferred: ZZ for integers, QQ for rationals, and polynomial rings such as ZZ[y] when other symbols appear in the coefficients.

p <- Poly(x^3 - 2 * x + 1, x)
p
#> Poly(x^3 - 2*x + 1, x, domain='ZZ')
Poly(x^2 + 2 * x * y + 1, x, y)
#> Poly(x^2 + 2*x*y + 1, x, y, domain='ZZ')
Poly(x^2 + y * x + 1, x)
#> Poly(x^2 + y*x + 1, x, domain='ZZ[y]')
Poly(x^2 + 1, x, modulus = 5)
#> Poly(x^2 + 1, x, modulus=5)

Polynomials support arithmetic, and the usual accessors return degree, coefficients, and monomials. as_expr() converts back to an expression.

q <- Poly(x^2 - 1, x)
p + q
#> Poly(x^3 + x^2 - 2*x, x, domain='ZZ')
p * q
#> Poly(x^5 - 3*x^3 + x^2 + 2*x - 1, x, domain='ZZ')
p^2
#> Poly(x^6 - 4*x^4 + 2*x^3 + 4*x^2 - 4*x + 1, x, domain='ZZ')
degree(p)
#> [1] 3
LC(p)
#> 1
all_coeffs(p)
#> [[1]]
#> 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 0
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> -2
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> 1
coeffs(p)
#> [[1]]
#> 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> -2
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> 1
monoms(p)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] 0
as_expr(p)
#> x^3 - 2*x + 1

Most functions accept plain expressions as well and convert internally.

degree(x^3 * y + x * y^4, y)
#> [1] 4
total_degree(x^3 * y + x * y^4)
#> [1] 5
coeff(3 * x^2 * y + x, x, 2)
#> 3*y

Division and greatest common divisors

div() returns the quotient and remainder, quo() and rem() return one of them. reduced() divides by several polynomials at once (multivariate division).

div(x^3 + 2 * x + 1, x - 1)
#> $q
#> x^2 + x + 3
#> 
#> $r
#> 4
quo(x^3 + 2 * x + 1, x - 1)
#> x^2 + x + 3
rem(x^3 + 2 * x + 1, x - 1)
#> 4
div(Poly(x^3 + 2 * x + 1, x), Poly(x^2 - 1, x))
#> $q
#> Poly(x, x, domain='ZZ')
#> 
#> $r
#> Poly(3*x + 1, x, domain='ZZ')
reduced(2 * x^4 + y^2 - x^2 + y^3, list(x^3 - x, y^3 - y))
#> $q
#> $q[[1]]
#> 2*x
#> 
#> $q[[2]]
#> 1
#> 
#> 
#> $r
#> x^2 + y^2 + y

gcd() and sym_lcm() work for univariate and multivariate polynomials. gcdex() solves the Bezout identity s f + t g = h, invert() computes an inverse modulo a polynomial, and cofactors() returns the GCD together with the cofactors.

gcd(x^2 - 1, x^2 + 2 * x + 1)
#> x + 1
gcd(x^2 * y - y, x * y^2 + y^2)
#> x*y + y
sym_lcm(x^2 - 1, x^2 + 2 * x + 1)
#> x^3 + x^2 - x - 1
gcdex(x^2 - 1, x^2 + 1)
#> $s
#> -1/2
#> 
#> $t
#> 1/2
#> 
#> $h
#> 1
invert(x^2 + 1, x^3 - 1)
#> -x^2/2 + x/2 + 1/2
cofactors(x^2 - 1, x - 1)
#> $h
#> x - 1
#> 
#> $cff
#> x + 1
#> 
#> $cfg
#> 1

Factorization

factor_sym() factors over the rationals by default, using Zassenhaus’ algorithm for univariate and Wang’s EEZ algorithm for multivariate polynomials.

factor_sym(x^6 - 1)
#> (x - 1)*(x + 1)*(x^2 - x + 1)*(x^2 + x + 1)
factor_sym(x^4 + 4)
#> (x^2 - 2*x + 2)*(x^2 + 2*x + 2)
factor_sym(x^2 * y^2 - x^2 - y^2 + 1)
#> (x - 1)*(x + 1)*(y - 1)*(y + 1)

Over an algebraic extension, the Gaussian integers, or a finite field \mathrm{GF}(p):

factor_sym(x^2 - 2, extension = sqrt(S(2)))
#> (x - sqrt(2))*(x + sqrt(2))
factor_sym(x^4 + 1, extension = sym_I)
#> (x^2 - I)*(x^2 + I)
factor_sym(x^3 + 2 * x + 2, modulus = 3)
#> x^3 - x - 1
factor_sym(x^5 + x + 1, modulus = 7)
#> (x - 2)*(x + 3)^2*(x^2 + 3*x - 2)

The first finite field example is irreducible modulo 3. Coefficients modulo p are printed in the symmetric range (-p/2, p/2].

factor_list() and sqf_list() return the factors with multiplicities.

str(lapply(sqf_list(x^5 - 2 * x^4 + x^3)$factors,
           function(f) list(sstr(f[[1]]), f[[2]])))
#> List of 2
#>  $ :List of 2
#>   ..$ : chr "x - 1"
#>   ..$ : num 2
#>  $ :List of 2
#>   ..$ : chr "x"
#>   ..$ : num 3

Resultants and discriminants

The resultant of two polynomials vanishes exactly when they have a common root; it eliminates a variable from a system. The discriminant vanishes when a polynomial has a repeated root.

resultant(x^2 - 1, x - 2, x)
#> 3
resultant(x^2 + y^2 - 1, x - y, x)
#> 2*y^2 - 1
discriminant(a * x^2 + b * x + c, x)
#> -4*a*c + b^2
discriminant(x^3 + a * x + b, x)
#> -4*a^3 - 27*b^2
subresultants(x^2 + 2 * x + 1, x^2 - 1)
#> [[1]]
#> x^2 + 2*x + 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> x^2 - 1
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> -2*x - 2

Groebner bases

groebner() computes a reduced Groebner basis with Buchberger’s algorithm. With the lexicographic order, the last element involves only the last variable, which is how polynomial systems are solved.

G <- groebner(list(x^2 + y^2 - 1, x - y), x, y, order = "lex")
vapply(G, sstr, "")
#> [1] "x - y"     "2*y^2 - 1"
G <- groebner(list(x * y - 1, x^2 + y^2 - 4), x, y, order = "lex")
vapply(G, sstr, "")
#> [1] "x + y^3 - 4*y"   "y^4 - 4*y^2 + 1"
G <- groebner(list(x^2 + y, x * y - 1), x, y, order = "grevlex")
vapply(G, sstr, "")
#> [1] "x^2 + y" "x*y - 1" "x + y^2"
is_zero_dimensional(list(x^2 + y^2 - 1, x - y), x, y)
#> [1] TRUE

Roots

roots() finds roots in closed form using formulas up to degree four and special methods for binomials, cyclotomic polynomials, and decomposable polynomials. It returns a list of roots with their multiplicities stored in the "multiplicity" attribute (SymPy returns a dictionary).

roots(x^2 - 3 * x + 2, x)
#> [[1]]
#> 2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 1
#> 
#> attr(,"multiplicity")
#> [1] 1 1
r <- roots((x - 1)^2 * (x + 3), x)
attr(r, "multiplicity")
#> [1] 1 2
roots(x^3 - 1, x)
#> [[1]]
#> 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> -1/2 - sqrt(3)*I/2
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> -1/2 + sqrt(3)*I/2
#> 
#> attr(,"multiplicity")
#> [1] 1 1 1
roots(x^4 + 1, x)
#> [[1]]
#> -sqrt(2)/2 - sqrt(2)*I/2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> -sqrt(2)/2 + sqrt(2)*I/2
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> sqrt(2)/2 - sqrt(2)*I/2
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> sqrt(2)/2 + sqrt(2)*I/2
#> 
#> attr(,"multiplicity")
#> [1] 1 1 1 1

all_roots() lists every root, repeated by multiplicity, as a plain list. real_roots() isolates the real roots exactly, nroots() approximates all roots numerically, and count_roots() counts the roots in an interval with Sturm sequences.

all_roots(Poly(x^4 - 1, x))
#> [[1]]
#> -1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 1
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> -I
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> I
real_roots(x^3 - 2 * x)
#> [[1]]
#> -sqrt(2)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 0
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> sqrt(2)
real_roots(x^5 - x + 1)
#> [[1]]
#> CRootOf(x^5 - x + 1, 0)
nroots(x^3 - x + 1, x)
#> [[1]]
#> -1.32471795724475
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 0.662358978622373 - 0.562279512062301*I
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> 0.662358978622373 + 0.562279512062301*I
count_roots(x^3 - 2 * x, x)
#> [1] 3
count_roots(x^4 - 1, x, -2, 0)
#> [1] 1
sturm(x^3 - 2 * x + 1, x)
#> [[1]]
#> x^3 - 2*x + 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 3*x^2 - 2
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> 4*x/3 - 1
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> 5/16
intervals(x^2 - 3)
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]][[1]]
#> -2
#> 
#> [[1]][[1]][[2]]
#> -1
#> 
#> 
#> [[1]][[2]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> [[2]][[1]][[1]]
#> 1
#> 
#> [[2]][[1]][[2]]
#> 2
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]][[2]]
#> [1] 1

CRootOf and RootSum

CRootOf(f, x, k) is the k-th root of f (real roots first, in increasing order), an exact object that can be evaluated numerically. RootSum() sums a function over all roots of a polynomial without computing them.

r0 <- CRootOf(x^5 - x + 1, x, 0)
r0
#> CRootOf(x^5 - x + 1, 0)
N(r0)
#> -1.16730397826142
CRootOf(x^2 - 2, x, 1)
#> CRootOf(x^2 - 2, 1)
RootSum(x^3 + x + 1, Lambda(x, x^2))
#> -2

The sum of the squares of the roots of x^3 + x + 1 is e_1^2 - 2e_2 = 0 - 2 = -2, found without solving the cubic.

Special polynomials and constructions 

cyclotomic_poly(12, x)
#> x^4 - x^2 + 1
legendre_poly(4, x)
#> 35*x^4/8 - 15*x^2/4 + 3/8
chebyshevt_poly(5, x)
#> 16*x^5 - 20*x^3 + 5*x
hermite_poly(4, x)
#> 16*x^4 - 48*x^2 + 12
swinnerton_dyer_poly(2, x)
#> x^4 - 10*x^2 + 1

horner() rewrites a polynomial for efficient evaluation, compose() and sym_decompose() compose and decompose polynomials, interpolate() finds the interpolating polynomial through points, and symmetrize() writes a symmetric polynomial in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials.

horner(x^3 + 2 * x^2 + 3 * x + 4, x)
#> x*(x*(x + 2) + 3) + 4
compose(x^2 + x, x - 1, x)
#> x^2 - x
sym_decompose(x^4 + 2 * x^3 - x - 1)
#> [[1]]
#> x^2 - x - 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> x^2 + x
interpolate(list(c(1, 1), c(2, 4), c(3, 9)), x)
#> x^2
symmetrize(x^2 + y^2)
#> [[1]]
#> -2*x*y + (x + y)^2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> 0
viete(x^2 + a * x + b, x)
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> r1 + r2
#> 
#> [[1]][[2]]
#> -a
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> r1*r2
#> 
#> [[2]][[2]]
#> b
monic(3 * x^2 + 6 * x + 9)
#> x^2 + 2*x + 3

symmetrize() shows x^2 + y^2 = (x + y)^2 - 2xy with a zero remainder. viete() gives Vieta’s formulas: r_1 + r_2 = -a and r_1 r_2 = b.

More classical polynomials, given by degree and variable, and the roots of Chebyshev polynomials:

chebyshevu_poly(3, x)
#> 8*x^3 - 4*x
hermite_prob_poly(3, x)
#> x^3 - 3*x
laguerre_poly(3, x)
#> -x^3/6 + 3*x^2/2 - 3*x + 1
jacobi_poly(2, 1, 2, x)
#> 21*x^2/4 - 3*x/2 - 3/4
chebyshevt_root(3, 1)
#> 0
chebyshevu_root(3, 1)
#> 0
symmetric_poly(2, list(x, y, a))
#> a*x + a*y + x*y

interpolating_poly() gives the Lagrange interpolating polynomial through given points, itermonomials() lists all monomials up to a total degree, and random_poly() draws integer coefficients at random (so its output depends on the R random seed).

expand(interpolating_poly(3, x, list(1, 2, 3), list(1, 4, 9)))
#> x^2
show <- function(l) vapply(l, sstr, "")
show(sym_ordered(itermonomials(list(x, y), 2)))
#> [1] "1"   "x"   "y"   "x^2" "y^2" "x*y"
set.seed(1)
random_poly(x, 3)
#> -7*x^3 - 4*x^2 - 10*x - 9

More polynomial functions

The functional interface mirrors the methods of Poly. LM() and LT() are the leading monomial and term, degree_list() gives the degree in each generator, poly_terms() lists the terms, and terms_gcd() pulls out the common monomial. content() and primitive() split off the integer content.

LM(4 * x^2 + 2 * x * y^2 + x * y + 3 * y, x, y)
#> x^2
LT(4 * x^2 + 2 * x * y^2 + x * y + 3 * y, x, y)
#> 4*x^2
degree_list(x^2 + y * x + 1)
#> [1] 2 1
vapply(poly_terms(x^2 + 2 * x * y^2 - y, x, y), function(t)
  paste0("(", paste(t$monom, collapse = ", "), "): ", sstr(t$coeff)), "")
#> [1] "(2, 0): 1"  "(1, 2): 2"  "(0, 1): -1"
terms_gcd(x^6 * y^2 + x^3 * y, x, y)
#> x^3*y*(x^3*y + 1)
content(2 * x + 4)
#> 2
show(primitive(2 * x + 4))
#>   content primitive 
#>       "2"   "x + 2"
is_polynomial(x^2 + 1, x)
#> [1] TRUE
is_polynomial(1 / x, x)
#> [1] FALSE

Exact and pseudo division: exquo() divides exactly, pdiv(), pquo(), and prem() divide after multiplying by a power of the leading coefficient so that no fractions appear, and pexquo() is the exact pseudo quotient. half_gcdex() returns half of the extended Euclidean algorithm, and gcd_list() and lcm_list() work on lists.

exquo(x^2 - 1, x - 1)
#> x + 1
show(pdiv(x^2 + 1, 2 * x - 4))
#>         q         r 
#> "2*x + 4"      "20"
pquo(x^2 + 1, 2 * x - 4)
#> 2*x + 4
prem(x^2 + 1, 2 * x - 4)
#> 20
pexquo(x^2 - 1, 2 * x - 2)
#> 2*x + 2
show(half_gcdex(x^4 - 2 * x^3 - 6 * x^2 + 12 * x + 15, x^3 + x^2 - 4 * x - 4))
#>           s           h 
#> "3/5 - x/5"     "x + 1"
gcd_list(list(x^3 - 1, x^2 - 1, x^2 - 3 * x + 2))
#> x - 1
lcm_list(list(x^3 - 1, x^2 - 1, x^2 - 3 * x + 2))
#> x^5 - x^4 - 2*x^3 - x^2 + x + 2

gff_list() is the greatest factorial factorization, sqf_norm() the square free norm over an algebraic extension, nth_power_roots_poly() a polynomial whose roots are the n-th powers of the roots of the input, ground_roots() the roots in the coefficient domain with multiplicities, and sym_trunc() reduces the coefficients modulo an integer into a symmetric range.

vapply(gff_list(x^5 + 2 * x^4 - x^3 - 2 * x^2), function(p)
  paste0("(", sstr(p[[1]]), ", ", p[[2]], ")"), "")
#> [1] "(x, 1)"     "(x + 2, 4)"
show(sqf_norm(x^2 - 2, sqrt(S(3)))[2:3])
#> [1] "x^2 - 2*sqrt(3)*x + 1" "x^4 - 10*x^2 + 1"
nth_power_roots_poly(x^4 - x^2 + 1, 2)
#> x^4 - 2*x^3 + 3*x^2 - 2*x + 1
minpoly(sqrt(S(2)) + sqrt(S(3)), x)
#> x^4 - 10*x^2 + 1
ground_roots(x^6 - 4 * x^4 + 4 * x^3 - x^2)
#> 0 1 
#> 2 2
sym_trunc(2 * x^3 + 3 * x^2 + 5 * x + 7, 3)
#> -x^3 - x + 1

poly_from_expr() and parallel_poly_from_expr() build Poly objects together with their options, hurwitz_conditions() and schur_conditions() give the stability conditions of a polynomial, and rootof() indexes the roots of a polynomial.

poly_from_expr(x^2 + 2 * x)[[1]]
#> Poly(x^2 + 2*x, x, domain='ZZ')
parallel_poly_from_expr(list(x^2 + 1, x * y))[[1]]
#> [[1]]
#> Poly(x^2 + 1, x, y, domain='ZZ')
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Poly(x*y, x, y, domain='ZZ')
show(hurwitz_conditions(x^3 + 2 * x^2 + 3 * x + 1))
#> [1] "2" "5" "1"
show(schur_conditions(x^2 + x / 2 + Rational(1, 4)))
#> [1] "18" "21"
rootof(x^3 - x - 1, x, 0)
#> CRootOf(x^3 - x - 1, 0)
show(refine_root(x^2 - 3, 1, 2, eps = 1e-2))
#> [1] "19/11" "26/15"

refine_root() shrinks an isolating interval of a real root, here around \sqrt 3 \approx 1.732. gff(), the greatest factorial factorization as an expression, is not implemented in SymPy either and signals an error:

tryCatch(gff(x^5 + 2 * x^4 - x^3 - 2 * x^2), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "symbolic falling factorial"

apart_list() returns the structure of a partial fraction decomposition, assemble_partfrac_list() turns it back into an expression, and numer() and denom() take a fraction apart.

pf <- apart_list((2 * x^3 - 2 * x) / (x^2 - 2 * x + 1))
assemble_partfrac_list(pf)
#> 2*x + 4 + 4/(x - 1)
numer((x + 1) / (x - 1))
#> x + 1
denom((x + 1) / (x - 1))
#> x - 1

Square free parts, Appell sequences and interpolation

sqf_part() is the square free part, the product of the distinct irreducible factors. gcdex_steps() lists the steps of the extended Euclidean algorithm as triples (s, t, r) with s f + t g = r.

sqf_part(x^3 - 3 * x - 2)
#> x^2 - x - 2
as_expr(sqf_part(Poly(x^3 - 3 * x - 2)))
#> x^2 - x - 2
gcdex_steps(x^4 - 2 * x^3 - 6 * x^2 + 12 * x + 15, x^3 + x^2 - 4 * x - 4)
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> 0
#> 
#> [[1]][[2]]
#> 1
#> 
#> [[1]][[3]]
#> x^3 + x^2 - 4*x - 4
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> 1
#> 
#> [[2]][[2]]
#> 3 - x
#> 
#> [[2]][[3]]
#> x^2 + 4*x + 3
#> 
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [[3]][[1]]
#> 3 - x
#> 
#> [[3]][[2]]
#> x^2 - 6*x + 10
#> 
#> [[3]][[3]]
#> 5*x + 5

The Appell sequences of sympy.polys.appellseqs:

bernoulli_poly(4, x)
#> x^4 - 2*x^3 + x^2 - 1/30
bernoulli_c_poly(4, x)
#> x^4 - 2*x^2 + 7/15
genocchi_poly(5, x)
#> -5*x^4 + 10*x^3 - 5*x
euler_poly(3, x)
#> x^3 - 3*x^2/2 + 1/4
andre_poly(4, x)
#> x^4 - 6*x^2 + 5

rational_interpolate() fits a rational function with a numerator of the given degree to data points:

rational_interpolate(list(c(1, 2), c(2, 3), c(3, 5), c(4, 7)), 2)
#> (2*x^2 - 3*x + 1)/(x - 1)
rational_interpolate(list(c(1, 2), c(2, 3), c(3, 5), c(4, 7)), 2, x = y)
#> (2*y^2 - 3*y + 1)/(y - 1)

PurePoly() is a polynomial that does not depend on the names of its generators, and solve_poly_system() solves a system of polynomial equations.

PurePoly(x^2 + 1) == PurePoly(y^2 + 1)
#> [1] TRUE
as_expr(PurePoly(x^2 + 1))
#> _0^2 + 1
degree(PurePoly(x^2 + 1, x))
#> [1] 2
solve_poly_system(list(x * y - 2 * y, 2 * y^2 - x^2), x, y)
#> [[1]]
#> (0, 0) 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> (2, -sqrt(2)) 
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> (2, sqrt(2))

PolyQuintic() holds the resolvents used to solve a quintic in radicals, and roots_quintic() returns the roots, or an empty list when the quintic is not solvable in radicals.

as_expr(PolyQuintic(x^5 - 5 * x + 12)$f20)
#> x^6 - 40*x^5 + 1000*x^4 - 20000*x^3 + 250000*x^2 - 66400000*x + 976000000
roots_quintic(x^5 - x + 1)
